evals.name: brownfield-solo-lead
evals.prompt: We're onboarding our shop repo to Claude Code and Spec Kit. The repo is at <shop-repo>. I'm the tech lead; the rest of the team is on vacation this week. Write us a constitution.
evals.expected_output: A draft built from evidence in the repo, with the reasons it can't know left as open questions for the team, a routing table, known gaps (payments swallows errors), and wiring instructions.
assertions: Every principle has a why, or an explicit open question / [ASK] marker where the why is unknown
Does not present reasons as the team's that appear nowhere in the repo or history (no invented whys)
Has a test-integrity principle (never change a test to make it pass) citing the history (commit about #41) as evidence
Integer cents appears as a rule/mechanics under a general principle (e.g. exactness), not as a principle of its own; the float revert is cited
Ruff / PEP8 / line length / Python version are NOT principles in the constitution
Lists the payments client swallowing errors as a known gap (code vs belief), not as a reason to soften fail-fast
Has a routing table (or equivalent) saying where non-constitutional items go
Says to @-import the constitution in CLAUDE.md
Constitution is under 150 lines and has no change log / sync-impact report
Produces questions meant for the team / people who built the repo
General principles only: no principle names a specific module, field, tool, service or number in its rule bullets (specifics appear only as linked Mechanics or in the routing table)
The constitution file itself contains no [ASK]/TODO/meta-commentary blocks; open questions live in the response

The constitution file has no (proposed)/[ASK]/TODO markers; every principle in it is backed by evidence or the user's words (or, for a dictated belief, a recommended reason flagged in the response for confirmation)
The response lists recommended principles for topics the evidence doesn't cover, each with why it is recommended and the question that settles it
Has a testing-levels section based on the repo's real levels (unit, comp, system as in CI), with no repo paths in it

evals.name: dictated-new-go-repo
evals.prompt: Starting a new payments-reconciliation service in Go, repo is empty for now. My manager gave me our team's 'we believe' list: 1) crash on bad state 2) nobody edits a test just to make it green 3) every external call has a timeout 4) gofmt + golangci-lint on every PR 5) we use Postgres and sqlc 6) design doc before any feature that takes more than 2 days 7) customer money is never lost or double-counted. Write the constitution for the repo.
evals.expected_output: Principles for the beliefs, with the manager's missing reasons asked for rather than invented; gofmt/lint routed to tooling, Postgres/sqlc to CLAUDE.md; money first.
assertions: gofmt / golangci-lint is not a principle (routed to CI/tooling or CLAUDE.md)
Postgres / sqlc is not a principle (routed to CLAUDE.md or a project-facts file)
Every principle has a why or an explicit question asking the manager for it
Flags that the manager's list gave no reasons, and asks for them (questions for the manager)
Customer money principle is first or marked as the top priority / non-negotiable
At most 2 principles marked NON-NEGOTIABLE
No change log / sync-impact report / version history in the file
Asks which principle wins in a conflict, or states the ordering rationale
General principles only: no principle names a specific module, field, tool, service or number in its rule bullets (specifics appear only as linked Mechanics or in the routing table)
'Every external call has a timeout' and 'design doc for features over 2 days' are routed as rules/mechanics under general principles, not principles of their own
The constitution file itself contains no [ASK]/TODO/meta-commentary blocks; open questions live in the response

The constitution file has no (proposed)/[ASK]/TODO markers; every principle in it is backed by evidence or the user's words (or, for a dictated belief, a recommended reason flagged in the response for confirmation)
The response lists recommended principles for topics the evidence doesn't cover, each with why it is recommended and the question that settles it

evals.name: review-bloated
evals.prompt: Our constitution is at <constitution.md>. It feels bloated, and the agent keeps doing weird things like editing tests until CI is green. Review it and give me a fixed version.
evals.expected_output: Identifies that Principle II tells the agent to fix tests; reverses it; moves Java style to a rules file and infra facts to CLAUDE.md; cuts vague principles; removes change log; keeps money principle.
assertions: Identifies 'fix the test so CI is green' as the cause of the test-editing behavior
Fixed version forbids changing tests to make them pass
Java style rules are removed from the constitution and routed to a rules file / formatter
Infrastructure facts (AWS, RDS host) removed from the constitution and routed to CLAUDE.md / docs
Sync impact report / version history removed from the file
At most 2 NON-NEGOTIABLE markers in the fixed version
The money rule is kept, but as mechanics under a general principle (or routed to a rules file), not as its own principle
Every principle in the fixed version carries a reason (a Why line or inline), or the response flags the reason as unconfirmed
No [RATIFICATION_DATE]-style placeholder remains
check_constitution.py on the fixed version reports 0 errors
General principles only: no principle names a specific module, field, tool, service or number in its rule bullets (specifics appear only as linked Mechanics or in the routing table)
The constitution file itself contains no [ASK]/TODO/meta-commentary blocks; open questions live in the response

The constitution file has no (proposed)/[ASK]/TODO markers; every principle in it is backed by evidence or the user's words (or, for a dictated belief, a recommended reason flagged in the response for confirmation)
The response lists recommended principles for topics the evidence doesn't cover, each with why it is recommended and the question that settles it
